newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq sanctions to stay unchanged after latest review.
newsitem.headline: Iraq sanctions to stay unchanged after latest review.

text.p: Tough economic sanctions imposed on Iraq since its 1990 invasion of Kuwait will remain unchanged on Friday when the Security Council conducts a routine 60-day review of the curbs, council members said.
The sanctions include a ban on the export of Iraqi oil and on most imports except for food, medicine and other humanitarian items.

A key condition for any easing of sanctions is a report by the U.N. Special Commission in charge of eliminating Iraq's weapons of mass destruction that Baghdad has disclosed full details of its nuclear, chemical, biological and ballistic missile programmes and that forbidden weapons and facilities have been scrapped.
In its last half-yearly report to the Security Council on Oct. 11, the commission said Iraq might still be hiding small but significant quantities of banned arms.

Iraq and the United Nations last May signed an agreement permitting Baghdad to export $2 billion of oil over renewable six-month periods to buy sorely needed food and medicine to ease the effects of sanctions on ordinary Iraqis.
But a number of factors have so far prevented this limited exception to sanctions from going into effect.

After Iraqi troops -- for the first time since the end of the 1991 Gulf War -- entered the largely Kurdish-inhabited north of the country at the end of August to back one side in an inter-Kurdish conflict, Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said security conditions in the region prevented the deployment of U.N. monitors to check on the oil-for-food scheme.
Iraq and the United Nations have also not yet reached agreement on freedom of movement for the U.N. teams and on conditions for U.N. recruitment of local employees.
Another major hurdle is that the Security Council's sanctions committee has yet to accept Iraq's latest formula for establishing the price of the oil it will be allowed to export.

The committee's decisions must be reached by consensus, in effect giving each of its 15 members a veto, and the United States in the past has withheld its assent. It apparently wishes to ensure that each oil contract is scrutinised by the committee instead of being given blanket approval under a pricing formula.
